prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength made frequency standards at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B043 as a single two-laureate prize and I am now more settled about it than in round 1. The scientific core is what I look for as a theorist embedded in experimental teams: a simple and original idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels for a narrow clock transition, which removed the central limitation of optical clocks and opened a new regime of precision. The result is robust in the sense that matters. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reached and compared across independent laboratories and species (Sr, Yb, Hg), and the same clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and bound varying constants and dark-matter couplings. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, Ye for taking the system to the accuracy frontier and for the many-body clock physics. No colleague has proposed a different laureate set for B043 in round 1, and the five supporters converge on the same two names. This is also the one candidate where the chair's questions on wording can be answered inside the citation itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. Precision timekeeping has been honoured in 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche), so the citation must make clear that the lattice and magic-wavelength concept is a distinct step and not a refinement of the comb or the ion clock. I think the wording above does this, but the committee should check it. Second, the priority record is not settled by our statements: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg, Hinkley and others contributed to early lattice clocks, and a two-name prize leaves them out; an outside reviewer should confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not treat it as a scientific criterion, but I accept that colleagues weigh it differently. Finally, I am less able to judge IceCube and moire physics than my colleagues, so my preference for B043 partly reflects the clarity of attribution and reproducibility, which I can judge, rather than a considered ranking of the physics in fields I know less well.

responses.point: Kroll asked whether my sixth place for the clocks in the opening ballot reflected merit or only the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and wants the citation to name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept explicitly.
responses.response: It was mainly my own field bias and a worry about overlap, not a judgement on merit. Reading round 1 changed my weighing: your point that the magic-wavelength lattice gives a many-atom, Doppler-free clock where the perturbation cancels by design, which neither the comb nor the single-ion clock provides, is what separates it from both earlier prizes. I have therefore written the citation around the lattice and the magic wavelength, and I still hold that the redefinition of the second is a policy milestone and should not count as support.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B010 as a discovery in the plainest sense, with Halzen and Karle, and asks whether waiting changes anything; he concedes attribution across AMANDA and IceCube is his main reservation.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously and I would not call IceCube a lesser result. In round 1 I said I could accept it as a serious competitor or a second part if the credit were settled. Having checked the arithmetic of the cap, a two-part prize pairing Katori and Ye with Halzen and Karle would need four names, which the rules forbid, and dropping to one name per part would not be defensible. Since the Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and AMANDA question is still open in the files, I keep B010 as my first alternative and would support it in a later year, or with expert advice that settles the credit.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B029 shows quantum mechanics producing a state nobody predicted in that form, and asks why a metrology advance whose headline consequence has not happened should outrank it.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge, and rewarding a new state of matter is as legitimate as rewarding a measurement tool. My difference with you is about stability rather than interest: the flat-band correlated phases are reproduced, but the pairing mechanism is debated and I find the evidence for quantitative understanding of the correlated states thinner than the frequency-ratio agreement between clock laboratories. I accept your reply that an unknown mechanism did not bar earlier superconductivity prizes, and I would be comfortable with B029 in a year or two, citing flat bands and correlated states. The Yuan Cao question must also be settled by an expert reviewer before I could support three names.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the Halperin, Nelson and Young theory of defect-mediated melting as a clean mechanism, overdue for recognition.
responses.response: I see the elegance and the three-person fit, and I agree it is a mechanism with a simple universal core. I remain outside my expertise here, and the issues that Kroll and Eriksson raise, that the hexatic phase is first-order or two-step depending on the system and that the 2016 prize already covers topological defects, are what keep me from moving. If the experimentalists and soft-matter members could agree on what exactly has been confirmed in nature, I would reconsider; at present B043 has the stronger evidence of agreement between independent measurements.

uncertainties: Whether an outside expert would confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair, given the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg and others.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice and magic-wavelength concept as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on citation wording.
Whether the redefinition of the second is treated by colleagues as a necessary condition or only a confirming milestone; I treat it as the latter.
Whether the Halzen, Karle, Yoshida credit for IceCube can be settled well enough to make B010 viable in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting circuits, so I recuse myself from decisions on circuit QED (B023) and probably B015 and B003; none of these is in my preferred configuration. I have no connection to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile, so no recusal is needed for B043. Kroll's institutional overlap with me through the WACQT leadership team is noted and is not relevant to B043. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
